title: What the Best Agents Share — Mardu Swanepoel, Flinn AI
talk_summary: Mardu Swanepoel identifies four patterns shared by strong agents: focus modes (constraining action/input space per task), transparent execution (showing plan, tool calls, and context to build trust and allow early intervention), personalization (playbooks, memory, skills to speed understanding of user intent), and reversibility (granular undo to bound the cost of mistakes). The talk is conceptual with product examples (Cursor, Claude, Harvey, Manifold) rather than measured results.

takeaways.what_they_do: Constrain each mode's tool set and system prompt to a narrow action space (planning mode writes no code; debug mode uses hypothesis-driven debugging with a dedicated debug server), so quality can be tuned and evaluated on a small surface first.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we put the agent in a specific mode where we constrain the action and the input space

takeaways.what_they_do: Harvey lets firms encode their methods and principles for reviewing a contract into a 'playbook' the agent follows, so output matches how the firm would do it rather than a generic answer.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you can create these playbooks in Harvey, and the agent would then do it in the same way as what your legal firm would have done it

takeaways.what_they_do: Surface the agent's to-do list, tool calls with inputs/outputs, and context sources so a human can stop a wrong trajectory at step two rather than after the final output.
takeaways.evidence_quote: it also enables the user to intervene at an earlier point in time if it sees the agent is really doing the wrong thing, and thereby reducing waste

takeaways.what_they_do: Harvey creates memories as the user instructs the agent and draws on them in later interactions, so repeated corrections are not re-taught each session.
takeaways.evidence_quote: it actually creates memories as we go along and as we instruct the agent, and it can then draw from that in subsequent interactions

takeaways.what_they_do: Cursor allows accept/reject at line, file, and conversation-checkpoint level, and parallel outputs from the same input across models, bounding the downside of any single agent action.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we're binding the cost of our mistakes

takeaways.technique: Speed to understanding over speed to output
takeaways.what_they_do: Optimize for the agent understanding implicit user intent (via playbooks, memory, skills) rather than emitting a fast but misaligned output.
takeaways.evidence_quote: they optimize for speed to outcome, but not speed to understanding
